questions.q: State the order and type of each matrix: (i) A = [2  −5  0  7], (ii) B = [[3], [−1], [4]], (iii) C = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], (iv) D = [[5, 0], [0, −2]].
questions.a: (i) Order 1 × 4, row matrix. (ii) Order 3 × 1, column matrix. (iii) Order 2 × 2, square matrix (not diagonal because off-diagonals 2, 3 ≠ 0). (iv) Order 2 × 2, diagonal matrix (square with off-diagonals zero). A wrong answer like "C is diagonal" reveals the student confuses "square" with "diagonal" — they must check aᵢⱼ = 0 for i ≠ j.

questions.q: A student writes: "Matrix M = [[0, 0], [0, 0]] is a diagonal matrix because all its diagonal elements are zero." Is this correct? Explain why or why not, referencing the definition.
questions.a: Yes, it is correct. The zero matrix of any square order satisfies the diagonal matrix condition: aᵢⱼ = 0 for all i ≠ j (vacuously true since all entries are zero). The definition does NOT require diagonal elements to be non-zero. A student who says "no, diagonal elements must be non-zero" has added an extra condition not in the definition — this is a common over-generalisation from seeing only non-zero diagonal examples.

questions.q: Construct a 3 × 3 diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the first three prime numbers. Then write its order and confirm it is diagonal by listing the (i, j) positions where the condition aᵢⱼ = 0 (i ≠ j) must hold.
questions.a: First three primes: 2, 3, 5. Matrix: [[2, 0, 0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 5]]. Order = 3 × 3. Off-diagonal positions: (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (2,3), (3,1), (3,2) — all six must be zero. A wrong construction like [[2, 0, 0], [3, 0, 0], [5, 0, 0]] reveals the student placed primes in the first column instead of the diagonal — they confuse "diagonal entries" with "first column entries".

questions.q: Matrix P is 4 × 4. Matrix Q is 1 × 4. Matrix R is 4 × 1. Which of the following sums are defined? (i) P + Q, (ii) Q + R, (iii) P + (transpose of Q). Justify each using order compatibility and matrix types.
questions.a: (i) Not defined: P is 4 × 4 (square), Q is 1 × 4 (row) — different orders. (ii) Not defined: Q is 1 × 4 (row), R is 4 × 1 (column) — different orders. (iii) Defined: Qᵀ is 4 × 1 (column), but P is 4 × 4 — still different orders, so NOT defined. Wait: Qᵀ is 4 × 1, P is 4 × 4 → not same order. So none are defined. A student who says (iii) is defined because "both have 4 rows" misses that columns must also match (4 vs 1). This tests understanding that addition requires identical order, not just same row count.

questions.q: A JEE-style question: "Let A be a 3 × 3 diagonal matrix with diagonal entries 1, 2, 3. Let B be the matrix obtained by interchanging the first and third rows of A. Is B diagonal? Is B square? Explain."
questions.a: A = diag(1, 2, 3) = [[1,0,0],[0,2,0],[0,0,3]]. Interchanging rows 1 and 3 gives B = [[0,0,3],[0,2,0],[1,0,0]]. B is square (3 × 3) but NOT diagonal because off-diagonal entries (1,3)=3, (3,1)=1 are non-zero. A student who says "B is diagonal because row operations preserve diagonal structure" is wrong — row operations destroy diagonal structure unless it's a scalar matrix. This tests the distinction between "square" (shape) and "diagonal" (pattern).

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario (Indian context: marks, prices, distances) that can be represented by a row matrix, a column matrix, a square matrix, and a diagonal matrix — all in one situation. Describe the data and the matrix for each type.
questions.a:
Scenario: A school canteen sells 3 items (samosa ₹15, chai ₹10, sandwich ₹30) over 3 days (Mon, Tue, Wed). 
- Row matrix (1 × 3): Prices of the 3 items on Monday = [15, 10, 30].
- Column matrix (3 × 1): Number of samosas sold on Mon, Tue, Wed = [[20], [25], [18]].
- Square matrix (3 × 3): Sales matrix where rows = items, columns = days, entry = quantity sold.
- Diagonal matrix (3 × 3): Profit per item per day if only diagonal days have profit (e.g., special offer days) = diag(500, 600, 450).
A poor answer uses the same matrix for all types or doesn't justify the structure — shows inability to map real data to matrix shapes.
